rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bahita means the defeated man was left speechless, unable to make a reply; the word has three forms, and ʿUrwa al-ʿUdhrī uses it for being stunned and silent.
rows.anchor: فبقي مغلوبا لا يجد مقالا ، ولا للمسألة جوابه

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi suggests God does not guide unbelievers to arguments or truth because they oppose them; al-Razi rejects this since no argument exists for unbelief to guide them toward.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي : يحتمل وجوها : منها أنه لا يهديهم لظلمهم وكفرهم للحجاج وللحق

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi proposes that injustice bars unbelievers from benefiting from additional divine favors; al-Razi says it is incoherent to say God withholds what is rationally impossible for them to receive.
rows.anchor: لا يهديهم لزيادات الألطاف من حيث أنهم بالكفر والظلم سدوا

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi reads the denial of guidance as denial of afterlife reward and Paradise; al-Razi rejects this because Paradise is absent from the context of reasoning and recognition.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي : ومنها أنه تعالى لا يهديهم إلى الثواب في الآخرة ولا يهديهم إلى الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In context, the proof was so clear that the opponent was silenced, yet it did not benefit him because God did not grant him guidance; this resembles the warning in 6:111.
rows.anchor: اللائق بسياق الآية أن يقال إنه تعالى لما بين أن الدليل كان قد بلغ في الظهور

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء وأبو علي الفارسي وأكثر النحويين
rows.claim: The preceding ألم تر is understood as ألم تر كالذي, so أو كالذي is coordinated by meaning: Have you considered the one who disputed Abraham, or the one who passed a town.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الكسائي والفراء وأبي علي الفارسي ، وأكثر النحويين قالوا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the kaf in أو كالذي as extra, yielding the sense ألم تر إلى الذي حاج والذي مر على قرية.
rows.anchor: والقول الثاني : وهو اختيار الأخفش : أن الكاف زائدة

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad supplies an omitted phrase: Have you considered the one who disputed Abraham and someone like the one who passed a town.
rows.anchor: والقول الثالث : وهو اختيار المبرد : أنا نضمر في الآية زيادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وأكثر المفسرين من المعتزلة
rows.claim: One reported view identifies the passer as an unbeliever who doubted resurrection.
rows.anchor: كان رجلا كافرا شاكا في البعث

rows.speaker: قتادة وعكرمة والضحاك والسدي
rows.claim: Those commentators identify the passer, whom they regard as a believer, as Ezra (Uzayr).
rows.anchor: وقال الباقون : إنه كان مسلما ، ثم قال قتادة وعكرمة والضحاك والسدي : هو عزير

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas through Ata identifies the passer as Jeremiah; some identify Jeremiah with al-Khidr, while Muhammad ibn Ishaq calls him a man of Aaron's tribe.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس : هو أرمياء ، ثم من هؤلاء من قال : إن أرمياء هو الخضر

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says Jeremiah was the prophet God sent when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and burned the Torah.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه : إن أرمياء هو النبي الذي بعثه الله عندما خرب بختنصر بيت المقدس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An argument for identifying the passer as an unbeliever is that his question sounds like someone who deems God's revival after death unlikely, which would be unbelief.
rows.anchor: حجة من قال : إن هذا المار كان كافرا وجوه الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection that the passer could have been prepubescent fails because God would not present a child's doubt as astonishing; al-Razi counters that the question may express ordinary improbability, not doubt in divine power.
rows.anchor: وهذه الحجة ضعيفة لاحتمال أن ذلك الاستبعاد ما كان بسبب الشك في قدرة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelief argument from فلما تبين له is weak: visible resurrection had not yet been shown, but that does not prove he lacked prior inferential knowledge.
rows.anchor: وهذا أيضا ضعيف لأن تبين الإحياء على سبيل المشاهدة ما كان حاصلا له قبل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that أعلم proves he learned God's power only then is weak; the witnessed event added certainty and reassurance without showing that he lacked the underlying knowledge earlier.
rows.anchor: وهذا أيضا ضعيف لأن تلك المشاهدة لا شك أنها أفادت نوع توكيد وطمأنينة ووثوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument that the passer was grouped with Nimrod is weak because Abraham's question about resurrection follows this story, making it fitting that the passer was a prophet like Abraham.
rows.anchor: أن هذا المار كان كافرا لانتظامه مع نمروذ في سلك واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer-prophet view argues that his question presupposes knowledge of God and of resurrection in principle, since singling out this case as astonishing makes sense only if resurrection is generally possible.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه كان عالما بالله ، وعلى أنه كان عالما بأنه تعالى يصح منه الإحياء في الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second argument for the passer's prophethood is that God directly asks how long he stayed, tells him the duration, and commands him to inspect the bones; the wording gives no basis to insert an angel or messenger.
rows.anchor: ظاهر هذا الكلام يدل على أن قائل هذه الأقوال معه هو الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that an angel or messenger relayed God's words departs from the apparent wording without evidence, so al-Razi rejects it.
rows.anchor: فصرف اللفظ عن هذا الظاهر إلى المجاز من غير دليل يوجبه غير جائز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third argument says that reviving the man, preserving his food and drink, and restoring his donkey are great honors unsuitable for an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وإعادة الحمار حيا بعد ما صار رميما مع كونه مشاهدا لإعادة أجزاء الحمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal that these wonders honored another prophet fails because the passage gives no mention or sign of such a prophet, though supporting that prophet would be the story's main point.
rows.anchor: ليس في هذه القصة حالة مشعرة بوجود النبي أصلا فلو كان المقصود من إظهار هذه الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that extraordinary signs may appear through someone whom God knows will later become a messenger, resolving the objection that the miracle preceded any prophetic claim.
rows.anchor: لو كان ذلك الشخص لكان إما أن يقال : إنه ادعى النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth argument treats ولنجعلك آية للناس as prophetic language, linked to 21:91; even if it does not explicitly confer prophethood, it promises great honor unsuitable for an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وهذا اللفظ إنما يستعمل في حق الأنبياء والرسل قال تعالى : { وجعلناها وابنها ءاية للعالمين }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative that the passer himself became a public sign through his unchanged youth is rejected: the wording promises to make him a sign after his revival, so it must mean more than the revival already witnessed.
rows.anchor: على أمر زائد عن هذا الإحياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi's second reply is that being made a sign entails great honor, which does not suit someone who died in unbelief and doubt about God's power.
rows.anchor: وذلك لا يليق بحال من مات على الكفر وعلى الشك في قدرة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas's occasion report says Nebuchadnezzar captured Israelites, including the scholar Ezra, who entered an abandoned town, wondered about its restoration by customary improbability, ate figs and grapes, drank juice, and slept.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما في سبب نزول الآية قال : إن بختنصر غزا بني إسرائيل فسبى منهم الكثيرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the report, God caused Ezra to die for a hundred years while young, concealed the death from people and animals, then revived him and asked how long he had remained dead.
rows.anchor: فأماته الله تعالى في منامه مائة عام وهو شاب ، ثم أعمى عن موته أيضا الإنس والسباع والطير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The report says Ezra saw unchanged figs, grapes, and drink, then his donkey's bones gathered, were reassembled, clothed with flesh and skin, and restored to life; Ezra prostrated and acknowledged God's power.
rows.anchor: فإذا هو عظام بيض تلوح وقد تفرقت أوصاله وسمع صوتا أيتها العظام البالية إني جاعل فيك روحا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: After a century, Jerusalem's people recognized Ezra as the man their fathers said had died in Babylon; he recited the Torah from memory, and it matched the recovered copy, prompting them to call him God's son.
rows.anchor: فلما أتاهم بعد مائة عام جدد لهم التوراة وأملاها عليهم عن ظهر قلبه لم يخرم منها حرفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi says the widely circulated report supports identifying the passer as a prophet.
rows.anchor: وهذه الرواية مشهورة فيما بين الناس ، وذلك يدل على أن ذلك المار كان نبيا

rows.speaker: وهب وقتادة وعكرمة والربيع
rows.claim: Wahb, Qatada, Ikrima, and al-Rabi identify the town as Jerusalem; Ibn Zayd instead identifies the town from which thousands fled fearing death.
rows.anchor: فقال وهب وقتادة وعكرمة والربيع : إيلياء وهي بيت المقدس ، وقال ابن زيد : هي القرية التي خرج منها الألوف حذر الموت

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asma'i explains khāwiyat as empty of inhabitants, with related uses for an empty belly, the Prophet's posture in prostration, a horse's stance, and stars setting without rain; ʿarsh is a roof or wooden building.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي : خوى البيت فهو يخوى خواء ممدود إذا ما خلا من أهله ، والخوا : خلو البطن من الطعام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas's description has the walls standing after the roofs collapsed, then the walls uprooted and falling onto the ruined roofs; the ruin is likened to uprooted palm stumps.
rows.anchor: أن حيطانها كانت قائمة وقد تهدمت سقوفها ، ثم انقعرت الحيطان من قواعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes على as عن, so the town is empty of its roofs, as in the expression about taking from people.
rows.anchor: جعل { على } بمعنى { عن } كقوله { إذا اكتالوا على الناس }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading says the town was ruined while its fruit trellises remained; that contrast makes the ruin more astonishing because such structures normally disappear in an empty town.
rows.anchor: أن المراد أن القرية خاوية مع كون أشجارها معروشة فكان التعجب من ذلك أكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passer's question means how or when God will restore the town; if he was a disbeliever it expresses doubt, while a prophet may mean customary improbability or request further confirmation, like Abraham.
rows.anchor: ومن قال كان نبيا حمله على الاستبعاد بحسب مجاري العرف والعادة أو كان المقصود منه طلب زيادة الدلائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here i.e. annā means from where or when; reviving the town means rebuilding it, as if he thought restoration would not occur, so God showed him a sign in his own person.
rows.anchor: والمراد بإحياء هذه القرية عمارتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hundred-year interval, rather than one day, makes revival more remote to reason and makes the changes he and others witness more astonishing.
rows.anchor: لأن الإحياء بعد تراخي المدة أبعد في العقول من الإحياء بعد قرب المدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baʿath means bringing him back to life; the Resurrection is named the Day of Baʿth, from raising a she-camel, and this wording indicates he returned as the same rational person prepared to reason about divine knowledge.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه عاد كما كان أولا حيا عاقلا فهما مستعدا للنظر والاستدلال

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i assimilate the consonants in كم لبثت; the remaining readers pronounce them distinctly, respectively because the articulations are close or distinct.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي بالإدغام والباقون بالإظهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All agree that God is the speaker of كم لبثت; the miraculous context and the passer's later sight of the donkey and decayed bones identify the speaker as God.
rows.anchor: أجمعوا على أن قائل هذا القول هو الله تعالى وإنما عرف أن هذا الخطاب من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's question does not seek information; it alerts the passer to the extraordinary events that have occurred.
rows.anchor: والجواب عنه : أن المقصود من هذا السؤال التنبيه على حدوث ما حدث من الخوارق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says a day or part of one because duration felt the same to a dead person, so he gave the shortest certain estimate; he died early in the day and then saw sunlight still remaining.
rows.anchor: أجاب بأقل ما يمكن أن يكون ميتا لأنه اليقين ، وفي التفسير أن إماتته كانت في أول النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His estimate was based on what seemed true to him, so it is not culpable lying; the sleepers of the cave similarly said they had stayed a day or part of one.
rows.anchor: أنه قال ذلك على حسب الظن ، ولا يكون مؤاخذا بهذا الكذب ، ونظيره أنه تعالى حكى عن أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph's brothers likewise spoke from an apparent sign when they said Joseph's brother had stolen the cup and that they testified only to what they knew.
rows.anchor: قال أخوة يوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stronger view is that the passer knew the interval resulted from death, since the purpose was to show resurrection and signs in himself or the donkey indicated death.
rows.anchor: الأظهر أنه علم أن ذلك اللبث كان بسبب الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported etymology derives ʿām from ʿawm, swimming, because a year involves a long passage through which one cannot act freely.
rows.anchor: وقيل : العام أصله من العوم الذي هو السباحة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم
rows.claim: These readers retain the hāʾ in connected recitation in لم يتسنه and the listed words اقتده، ماليه، سلطانيه، ماهيه; Hamza omits it throughout, while al-Kisa'i omits it in the first two and retains it in the others.
rows.anchor: فقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر وعاصم هذه الحروف كلها بإثبات الهاء في الوصل

rows.speaker: كثير من الناس
rows.claim: Many derive سنة from سنوة; on that account its hāʾ in لم يتسنه is a pause marker, supported by forms such as سنوات, سانيت, and a poetic use of مسنتون.
rows.anchor: من السنة وزعم كثير من الناس أن أصل السنة سنوة

rows.speaker: الفراء عن الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Farra, quoted by al-Wahidi, allows سنة to derive from سننة; then لم يتسنه comes from لم يتسنن, with a final nūn dropped and a pause hāʾ added, like لم يتقضه.
rows.anchor: نقل الواحدي عن الفراء أنه قال : يجوز أن تكون أصل سنة سننة

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi derives the word from مسنون, related to pouring; the drink remained undiminished, with the final nūn dropped and pause hāʾ supplied.
rows.anchor: والسن في اللغة هو الصب ، هكذا قال أبو علي الفارسي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For readers retaining the hāʾ, سنة derives from سنهه, supported by the diminutive سنيهة and the verb سانهت; hāʾ is a root consonant, not a pause marker.
rows.anchor: والسنة أصلها سنهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لم يتسنه means the food and drink did not change; literally, the years did not pass over it, as though time had not touched it, while Abu Ali's account also permits the sense that the drink did not dry up.
rows.anchor: أي لم يأت عليه السنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unchanged food seems to support his short estimate, but this strengthens the lesson: the donkey's decayed bones then show God's power, since food usually spoils sooner than a donkey's remains.
rows.anchor: فحينئذ يعظم اشتياقك إلى الدليل الذي يكشف عن هذه الشبهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing perishable food preserved while bones had decayed and were then revived made the wonder more vivid and firmly established the proof in his mind.
rows.anchor: فرأى ما لا يبقى باقيا ، وهو الطعام والشراب ، وما يبقى غير باق وهو العظام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although لم يتسنه grammatically follows drink, food too can be described as unchanged, especially delicate food that spoils quickly; the reported food was figs and grapes, with grape juice and milk.
rows.anchor: كما يوصف الشراب بأنه لم يتغير ، كذلك يوصف الطعام بأنه لم يتغير

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's reading has وانظر إلى طعامك وهذا in the passage about inspecting the food.
rows.anchor: قراءة ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The donkey's bones alone do not prove a hundred years, because God could make them decay instantly; their restoration to life is the miracle confirming the report of the duration.
rows.anchor: لأنه لما شاهد انقلاب العظام النخرة حيا في الحال علم أن القادر على ذلك قادر

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says the revival after death demonstrated the truth of resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك : معنى قوله أنه لما أحيى بعد الموت كان دليلا على صحة البعث

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another reported view says the sign was that the man returned young with black hair while his grandsons were old, with white beards and hair.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره : كان آية لأن الله تعالى أحياه شابا أسود الرأس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making him a sign means honoring him and promising high religious and worldly rank, which is unsuitable for someone who died in unbelief and doubt.
rows.anchor: المراد منه التشريف والتعظيم والوعد بالدرجة العالية في الدين والدنيا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains the coordinating waw in ولنجعلك by an implied فعلنا ما فعلنا; otherwise looking at the donkey would be a condition for making him a sign.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : دخلت الواو لأنه فعل بعدها مضمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same implied-clause construction appears in 6:105 and 6:75: God made the signs or showed Abraham the kingdom for the stated purpose.
rows.anchor: ومثله قوله تعالى : { وكذالك نصرف الايات وليقولوا درست }

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators take the bones to be the donkey's bones; the lām in إلى العظام stands in place of a pronoun.
rows.anchor: فأكثر المفسرين على أن المراد بالعظام عظام حماره ، فإن اللام فيه بدل الكناية

rows.speaker: قتادة والربيع وابن زيد
rows.claim: Qatada, al-Rabi, and Ibn Zayd identify the bones as the man's own, with his head and eyes revived while his remaining body reassembled; al-Razi rejects this as inconsistent with his estimate of one day and the whole-person wording.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول قتادة والربيع وابن زيد ، وهو عندي ضعيف لوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: How means revive; God is said to نشر the dead, and 80:22 and 36:78–79 speak of reviving bones.
rows.anchor: وصف الله العظام بالإحياء في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: A reading ننشرها with nūn and shīn means spreading after folding: lifelessness is like being folded, and life restores active movement.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : كأنه ذهب إلى النشر بعد الطي

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ننشزها with zāy, meaning to raise the bones, return each to its place, and join them together.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي { كيف ننشزها } بالزاي المنقوطة من فوق

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakha'i reads ننشزها with an active causative form; al-Akhfash explains it as raising, the same sense as the other readings.
rows.anchor: وروي عن النخعي أنه كان يقرأ { ننشزها } بفتح النون وضم الشين والزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readings describe God arranging the bones in order, then spreading flesh, veins, nerves, and skin over them and raising each part beside the next.
rows.anchor: والمعنى من جميع القراءات أنه تعالى ركب العظام بعضها على بعض حتى اتصلت

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted subject after فلما تبين له, namely that God can do all things; al-Razi calls this strained and says the phrase refers to witnessed revival.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب ( الكشاف ) : فاعل { تبين له } مضمر تقديره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After directly witnessing death and revival, the man says he knows God can do all things; the experience confirms and renews knowledge he already had by inference.
rows.anchor: بل الصحيح أنه لما تبين له أمر الإماتة والإحياء على سبيل المشاهدة

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read قال أعلم as an imperative; one explanation is that after the sign he commands himself to know this truth.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي { قال أعلم } على لفظ الأمر وفيه وجهان أحدهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the birds were slaughtered, plucked, cut up and mixed, with their heads kept; parts were put on four mountains, and at Abraham's call they reassembled and came alive by God's permission.
rows.anchor: روي أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أمر بذبحها ونتف ريشها وتقطيعها جزءا جزءا

rows.speaker: عاصم في رواية أبي بكر والفضل
rows.claim: Asim, in the transmissions of Abu Bakr and al-Fadl, reads جزءا with a heavier hamza where it occurs; the other readers use the lighter form, and both mean a portion.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم في رواية أبي بكر والفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some explain سعيا as running or walking on their feet; the alternative of flight is linguistically weak because birds are not said to perform saʿy when flying.
rows.anchor: فقيل عدوا ومشيا على أرجلهن ، لأن ذلك أبلغ في الحجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others defend the flight reading by defining saʿy as rapid movement, whether the movement is walking or flying.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من أجاب عنه بأن السعي هو الاشتداد في الحركة

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi's school argues the verse shows bodily structure is not a necessary condition for life: separated pieces understood the call and could move toward Abraham.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحابنا بهذه الآية على أن البنية ليست شرطا في صحة الحياة

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi argues the verse shows a body is necessary for life because cutting the birds apart ended their lives.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي : الآية دالة على أنه لا بد من البنية من حيث أوجب التقطيع بطلان حياتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Razi answers that simultaneous occurrence does not prove necessary connection; the separated parts' understanding and movement show life can exist without an assembled body.
rows.anchor: لأن حصول المقارنة لا يدل على وجوب المقارنة ، أما الانفكاك عنه في بعض الأحوال فإنه يدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aziz means dominant over all possible things, and hakim means knowing the outcomes and ends of things.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى أنه غالب على جميع الممكنات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing knowledge of God and resurrection, the passage turns to laws and obligations, beginning with the duties involved in spending wealth.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر من بيان أصول العلم بالمبدأ وبالمعاد ومن دلائل صحتهما ما أراد أتبع ذلك

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi sees 2:261 as explaining the abundant multiplication promised in 2:245; the resurrection proofs in between establish why spending is not futile, since God rewards a single seed with seven hundred grains.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي رحمه الله : إنه تعالى لما أجمل

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm says the seed parable follows the proof of the Prophet to encourage giving wealth and risking oneself to support him and establish his law.
rows.anchor: وهو أنه تعالى ضرب هذا المثل بعد أن احتج على الكل بما يوجب تصديق النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed connection contrasts the believer's spending in God's way with the unbeliever's spending in the way of false patrons, following the preceding contrast in guardianship.
rows.anchor: لما بين تعالى أنه ولي المؤمنين ، وأن الكفار أولياؤهم الطاغوت بين مثل ما ينفق المؤمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted comparison is either the likeness of the spenders' donations to a seed or the likeness of a farmer planting a seed.
rows.anchor: المسألة الثانية : في الآية إضمار ، والتقدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spending in God's way means spending for His religion: some limit it to jihad, while others include all good, obligatory and voluntary spending for migration, jihad, charity, and public benefit.
rows.anchor: قيل : أراد النفقة في الجهاد خاصة

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says the parable works even if no real ear has one hundred grains: anyone seeking worldly profit would plant one grain for a seven-hundredfold return, and the same logic should motivate afterlife reward.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول القفال رحمه الله وهو حسن جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative claim that such a spikelet was seen in millet is extremely weak.
rows.anchor: والجواب الثاني : أنه شوهد ذلك في سنبلة الجاورس ، وهذا الجواب في غاية الركاكة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Abu Amr, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i assimilate the t in أنبتت with the s in سبع because both letters are voiceless; the others pronounce both distinctly.
rows.anchor: كان أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي يدغمون التاء في السين في قوله { أنبتت سبع سنابل }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not specify the amount of God's multiplication or who receives it; it may encompass all the pious or distinguish some for greater sincerity or divine acceptance.
rows.anchor: وليس فيه بيان كمية تلك المضاعفة ، ولا بيان من يشرفه الله بهذه المضاعفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is vast in power to reward generously according to the amount and kind of spending, so no worker's deed is lost.
rows.anchor: أي واسع القدرة على المجازاة على الجود والافضال عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse was revealed concerning Uthman and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf: Uthman equipped the Tabuk expedition with a thousand camels and a thousand dinars, while Abd al-Rahman gave half his wealth, four thousand dinars.
rows.anchor: نزلت الآية في عثمان وعبد الرحمن بن عوف ، أما عثمان فجهز جيش العسرة في غزوة تبوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet prayed that God be pleased with Uthman after his contribution.
rows.anchor: فرفع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يديه يقول

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators distinguish the previous verse as spending on oneself and this verse as spending on others, whose reward requires no taunting or harm.
rows.anchor: إن الآية المتقدمة مختصة بمن أنفق على نفسه ، وهذه الآية بمن أنفق على غيره

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says the condition also covers someone spending on himself to join the Prophet and Muslims in jihad: he must not boast to them or insult fellow believers.
rows.anchor: وذلك هو أن ينفق على نفسه ويحضر الجهاد مع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Minn can mean benefaction; Ibn al-Anbari cites a poem asking someone to favor the speaker with a greeting, and the Prophet called Abu Bakr the most generous companion in wealth.
rows.anchor: في اللغة على وجوه أحدها : بمعنى الانعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Minn can also mean diminishing or withholding; the Quran describes a reward as غير ممنون, and death is called manun because it cuts lives short.
rows.anchor: النقص من الحق والبخس له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blameworthy minn is publicizing one's benefaction, while adhā is reproaching the recipient because of what was given.
rows.anchor: المن هو إظهار الاصطناع إليهم ، والأذى شكايته منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taunting deepens the needy recipient's humiliation and turns a prior benefit into harm after the giver has helped him.
rows.anchor: زاد ذلك في انكسار قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Publicizing generosity discourages people in need from seeking the giver's charity.
rows.anchor: إظهار المن يبعد أهل الحاجة عن الرغبة في صدقته إذا اشتهر من طريقه ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A giver should recognize the gift as God's favor, be grateful for being enabled to give, and fear that some accompanying behavior may prevent acceptance.
rows.anchor: وأن يعتقد أن لله عليه نعما عظيمة حيث وفقه لهذا العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deeper reason is that God prepared the means of giving and removed its obstacles, so God is the true giver; fixating on visible causes instead of God leaves one at an animal level.
rows.anchor: ومتى كان الأمر كذلك كان المعطي هو الله في الحقيقة لا العبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adhā here should mean the reproach attached to the gift, not every hurt to a believer; an example is telling the poor person that his visits distress the giver.
rows.anchor: مثل أن يقول للفقير : أنت أبدا تجيئني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One who gives without either taunt or harm receives great reward and abundant recompense.
rows.anchor: من أنفق ماله ثم أنه لا يتبعه المن والأذى فله الأجر العظيم والثواب الجزيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording requires avoiding both taunt and harm in the sense that neither may occur; the reward is not preserved merely by avoiding one while committing the other.
rows.anchor: بل الشرط أن لا يوجد واحد منهما

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Mu'tazila infer that major sins cancel reward, since the promised reward remains only when minn and adhā are absent.
rows.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : الآية دالة على أن الكبائر تحبط ثواب فاعلها

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi's school says taunting and harm show the gift was given for self-exaltation, not God's pleasure, so it never earned reward in the first place.
rows.anchor: المراد من الآية أن حصول المن والأذى يخرجان الانفاق من أن يكون فيه أجر وثواب أصلا

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi objects that ثم makes taunting later than a valid act of giving, which should already have earned reward because a condition must exist when its cause occurs.
rows.anchor: طعن القاضي في هذا الجواب فقال

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: The response is that later taunting reveals the original gift was made for status, not God; alternatively, a later opposing event may prevent an earlier act from taking effect, as in the doctrine of ultimate outcome.
rows.anchor: إلا أن هذا الذكر المتأخر يدل ظاهرا على أنه حين أنفق ما كان إنفاقه لوجه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that both taunting and harm are major sins because either one strips this great act of its promised reward.
rows.anchor: حيث تخرج هذه الطاعة العظيمة بسبب كل واحد منهما

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Mu'tazila say the servant's action makes God owe him reward; al-Razi's school says reward comes through God's promise, since performing an obligation does not itself earn payment.
rows.anchor: احتجت المعتزلة بهذه الآية على أن العمل يوجب الأجر على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi's school argues this verse disproves cancellation of reward because it states without qualification that the spenders have their reward, even after grave sins.
rows.anchor: احتج أصحابنا بهذه الآية على نفي الإحباط

rows.speaker: الأمة
rows.claim: The community agrees that having their reward with their Lord is conditioned on not committing unbelief; this shows a general expression may intend a restricted class.
rows.anchor: أجمعت الأمة على أن قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since general wording may be restricted, general texts cannot provide categorical proof for the Mu'tazili doctrine of irrevocable threats.
rows.anchor: لم تكن دلالة اللفظ العام على الاستغراق دلالة قطعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading says their spending is not wasted: its reward will be fully delivered on the Day of Resurrection, so they neither fear nor grieve over losing it.
rows.anchor: لا يضيع ، بل ثوابه موفر عليهم يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading is that they will not fear punishment on the Day of Resurrection, as in the assurances in 27:89 and 21:103.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد أنهم يوم القيامة لا يخافون العذاب ألبتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A recognized word is speech accepted by hearts and not rejected; here it means answering a petitioner kindly, while Ata glosses it as a good promise.
rows.anchor: القول الذي تقبله القلوب ولا تنكره

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata explains قول معروف as a good promise to the petitioner.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء : عدة حسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maghfira may mean forgiving a poor person's harsh words when refused, since disappointment can provoke a sharp response.
rows.anchor: أن الفقير إذا رد بغير مقصوده شق عليه ذلك ، فربما حمله ذلك على بذاءة اللسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maghfira may mean receiving God's forgiveness for refusing the petitioner kindly.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : أن يكون المراد ونيل مغفرة من الله بسبب الرد الجميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maghfira may mean concealing the needy person's circumstances and not exposing his need to someone he would rather avoid.
rows.anchor: أن يستر حاجة الفقير ولا يهتك ستره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading addresses the person asked with قول معروف and the petitioner with مغفرة: the petitioner should excuse a refusal when the requested help is unavailable.
rows.anchor: خطاب مع السائل بأن يعذر المسؤول في ذلك الرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kind refusal is better than a gift followed by abuse because that combines benefit with harm, and the harm may outweigh the benefit; kind words bring joy without injury.
rows.anchor: وربما لم يف ثواب الانفاع بعقاب الإضرار

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Some say the verse concerns voluntary charity, because obligatory alms cannot be withheld or refused; al-Razi allows it to include obligatory charity redirected to another petitioner or poor person.
rows.anchor: إن الآية واردة في التطوع ، لأن الواجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is independent of people's charity and commands it to reward them; He is forbearing in delaying punishment for those who taunt and harm recipients.
rows.anchor: عن صدقة العباد فإنما أمركم بها ليثيبكم عليها

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi says the prohibition clarifies that taunting and harm cancel the reward, not the already completed act of charity; the verse compares this cancellation with a clearer case.
rows.anchor: فالمراد إبطال أجرها وثوابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first parable compares the taunting donor to a show-off who is also an unbeliever, whose reward's failure is clearer than the donor's.
rows.anchor: لأن بطلان أجر نفقة هذا المرائي الكافر أظهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The smooth stone is the unbeliever, the thin soil is the apparent donation, and the downpour is unbelief or taunting that washes away the deed's reward.
rows.anchor: فالكافر كالصفوان ، والتراب مثل ذلك الإنفاق

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i argues that reward and punishment cannot both be deserved because each is an eternal pure benefit or harm; otherwise the same outcome would be both just punishment and unjust denial of reward.
rows.anchor: فلو استحق ثواب طاعته وعقاب معصيته لوجب أن يستحق النقيضين

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Al-Razi's school reads لا تبطلوا as a command not to perform charity in a null form: if the original motive was other than God, no valid reward ever arose to be removed later.
rows.anchor: بل المراد به أن يأتي بهذا العمل باطلا

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: If old and new merits do not conflict, the new event cannot erase the old; if they do conflict, the new event has no priority, and prevention is easier than reversal.
rows.anchor: إن لم يكن بينهما منافاة لم يلزم من طريان الطارىء زوال النافي

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: A later event cannot erase what existed only in the past, what exists now without contradiction, or what has not yet come into existence.
rows.anchor: في الوجود في الماضي وهو محال

rows.speaker: أصحابنا
rows.claim: Explaining the prior merit's disappearance by the arrival of the later event is circular, since the later event requires the prior resistance already to have disappeared.
rows.anchor: فلو جعلنا زوال النافي معللا بطريان الطارىء لزم الدور وهو محال

rows.speaker: أبو هاشم
rows.claim: Abu Hashim's mutual-balancing account has each event erase some of the other; if both resulting absences occur, the causes must simultaneously exist and not exist, an impossibility.
rows.anchor: والأول هو الموازنة وهو قول أبي هاشم وهو باطل

rows.speaker: أبو علي الجبائي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Jubba'i says the later punishment alone removes prior reward; al-Razi objects that the earlier good then provides no benefit or protection, contrary to 99:7 and justice.
rows.anchor: وأما الثاني : وهو قول أبي علي الجبائي فهو أيضا باطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a minor sin cancels only some equal parts of reward, selecting those parts without a distinguishing cause is arbitrary; if it cancels all reward, that is rejected by agreement, so minor sins cancel none.
rows.anchor: فالصغيرة الطارئة إذا انصرف تأثيرها إلى بعض تلك الاستحقاقات دون البعض مع استواء الكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a major punishment exceeds prior reward, one part cannot be singled out to cancel it without cause; if every part independently cancels it, multiple independent causes produce the same effect, which is impossible.
rows.anchor: والقسم الثاني باطل ، لأنه حينئذ يجتمع على إبطال الجزء الواحد من الثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good and blameworthy consequences can coexist without erasing each other: a servant who saves his master from an enemy deserves praise but also blame for exposing the master's property to theft.
rows.anchor: فاشتغل العبد بمحاربة ذلك العدو وقتله فذلك الفعل من العبد يستوجب استحقاقه للمدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A later act cannot alter the causal force of an earlier act in the past; absent such an effect, the earlier entitlement remains, and the past is stronger than a later event.
rows.anchor: لأن ذلك الفعل إنما يكون موجودا في الزمان الماضي
